danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Mens dette foregik i Petersborg, havde franskmændene allerede passeret Smolensk og nærmede sig mere og mere Moskva. Napoleons historieskriver Thiers forsøger, ligesom hans andre historieskrivere, at retfærdiggøre sin helt ved at sige, at han blev draget mod Moskvas mure mod sin vilje. Han har lige så ret som andre historikere, der søger forklaringen på historiske begivenheder i én mands vilje; han har lige så ret som de russiske historikere, der hævder, at Napoleon blev lokket til Moskva ved de russiske kommandanters dygtighed. Her griber — foruden den retrospektive lov, der ser alt det forgangne som en forberedelse til de begivenheder, der siden indtraf — gensidigheden ind og forvirrer det hele. En god skakspiller, der har tabt et parti, er oprigtigt overbevist om, at hans tab skyldtes en fejl, han begik, og leder efter den fejl i åbningen, men glemmer, at der på hvert trin i partiet var lignende fejl, og at ingen af hans træk var perfekte. Han bemærker kun den fejl, han retter opmærksomheden mod, fordi hans modstander udnyttede den. Hvor meget mere indviklet er krigens spil, der udspiller sig inden for bestemte tidsrammer, og hvor det ikke er én vilje, der styrer livløse genstande, men alt er resultatet af utallige sammenstød mellem forskellige viljer!

Efter Smolensk søgte Napoleon et slag hinsides Dorogobuzj ved Vjazma og derefter ved Tsarevo-Zajmisjtje, men det skete, at på grund af et sammentræf af utallige omstændigheder kunne russerne ikke levere slag, før de nåede Borodino, halvfjerds verst fra Moskva. Fra Vjazma beordrede Napoleon direkte march mod Moskva.

Moscou, la capitale asiatique de ce grand empire, la ville sacrée des peuples d'Alexandre, Moscou avec ses innombrables églises en forme de pagodes chinoises, * dette Moskva gav Napoleons fantasi ingen ro. På marchen fra Vjazma til Tsarevo-Zajmisjtje red han på sin lette, brune stubhalede pasgænger, ledsaget af sin garde, sit livvagt, sine pager og adjudanter. Berthier, hans stabschef, blev tilbage for at udspørge en russisk fange, taget af kavaleriet. Fulgt af Lelorgne d'Ideville, en tolk, indhentede han Napoleon i galop og holdt sin hest an med et morskabsfuldt udtryk.
* »Moskva, dette store imperiums asiatiske hovedstad, det hellige byen for Aleksanders folk, Moskva med sine utallige kirker formet som kinesiske pagoder.«
»Nå?« spurgte Napoleon.
»En af Platovs kosakker siger, at Platovs korps forener sig med hovedhæren, og at Kutuzov er udnævnt til øverstkommanderende. Han er en meget snedig og snakkesalig fyr.«

Napoleon smilede og bød dem give kosakken en hest og bringe manden til ham. Han ønskede selv at tale med ham. Flere adjudanter galoperede af sted, og en time senere red Lavrusjka (Denisovs livegne tjener, som han havde overdraget Rostov), op til Napoleon i en ordonnansfrakke og på en fransk kavalerisadel, med et muntert og bedugget ansigt. Napoleon bød ham ride ved sin side og begyndte at udspørge ham.
»Er du kosak?«
»Ja, kosak, Deres Nåde.«

»Kosakken, der ikke vidste, i hvilket selskab han befandt sig — for Napoleons jævne fremtoning havde intet, der kunne røbe for et orientalsk sind, at en monark var nærværende — talte med yderste fortrolighed om krigens begivenheder,« siger Thiers i sin beretning om denne episode. I virkeligheden var Lavrusjka, der dagen før var blevet fuld og havde efterladt sin herre uden middagsmad, blevet pisket og sendt til landsbyen for at skaffe høns, hvor han var gået i gang med at plyndre, indtil franskmændene tog ham til fange. Lavrusjka var en af de grove, frække lakajer, der har set alting, anser det for nødvendigt at gøre alting på en udspekuleret og lusket måde, er rede til at yde enhver tjeneste for deres herre og er ivrige efter at gætte deres herres laveste drifter, især dem der udspringer af forfængelighed og småskårenhed.
Da han befandt sig i Napoleons selskab, hvis identitet han let og sikkert genkendte, var Lavrusjka ikke det mindste forfjamsket, men gjorde blot sit yderste for at vinde sin nye herres gunst.

Han vidste udmærket godt, at dette var Napoleon, men Napoleons tilstedeværelse kunne ikke mere skræmme ham end Rostovs eller en sergents med riset ville have kunnet, for han havde intet, som hverken sergenten eller Napoleon kunne fratage ham.

Så han snakkede løs og fortalte alt det sladder, han havde hørt blandt ordonnanserne. Meget af det var sandt. Men da Napoleon spurgte ham, om russerne mente, de ville slå Bonaparte eller ej, klemte Lavrusjka øjnene sammen og tænkte sig om.
I dette spørgsmål så han fiffig snedighed, som den slags mænd ser snedighed i alt, og så han rynkede panden og svarede ikke straks.
»Det er sådan,« sagde han betænksomt, »hvis der snart bliver et slag, vil jeres vinde. Det er sikkert. Men går der tre dage, ja — så vil det samme slag ikke snart være overstået.«

Lelorgne d'Ideville fortolkede smilende denne tale for Napoleon således: »Finder et slag sted inden de næste tre dage, vinder franskmændene, men sker det senere, véd kun Gud hvad der sker.« Napoleon smilede ikke, skønt han tydeligvis var i strålende humør, og han beordrede ordene gentaget.
Lavrusjka bemærkede dette og tilføjede for yderligere at underholde ham, idet han lod som om han ikke vidste, hvem Napoleon var:
»Vi véd, at I har Bonaparte, og at han har slået alle i hele verden, men vi er en anden sag ...« — uden at vide hvorfor eller hvordan dette stykke pralende patriotisme gled ud til sidst.

Tolken oversatte disse ord uden den sidste sætning, og Bonaparte smilede. »Den unge kosak fik sin mægtige samtalepartner til at smile,« siger Thiers. Efter at have redet et par skridt i tavshed vendte Napoleon sig til Berthier og sagde, at han ønskede at se, hvordan nyheden om at han talte med kejseren selv — med den selvsamme kejser, der havde skrevet sit udødeligt sejrrige navn på pyramiderne — ville påvirke dette enfant du Don. *
* »Barn af Don.«
Meddelelsen blev derefter givet videre til Lavrusjka.

Lavrusjka, der forstod at dette blev gjort for at forvirre ham, og at Napoleon forventede, han ville blive forskrækket, lod for at behage sine nye herrer straks som om han var forbløffet og lamslået, spilede øjnene op og antog det udtryk, han normalt satte op, når han blev ført hen for at blive pisket. »Så snart Napoleons tolk havde talt,« siger Thiers, »greb forbavselse kosakken, og han sagde ikke et ord mere, men red videre med blikket fæstnet på erobreren, hvis berømmelse var nået til ham over Østens stepper. Al hans snaksomhed var pludselig afbrudt og erstattet af en naiv og tavs følelse af beundring. Napoleon lod kosakken forære en gave og satte ham derefter fri som en fugl, der vender tilbage til sine hjemlige marker.«

Napoleon red videre og drømte om det Moskva, der så stærkt tiltrak hans fantasi, og »fuglen, der vendte tilbage til sine hjemlige marker« galoperede hen til vore forposter og opdigtede undervejs alt det, der ikke var sket, men som han agtede at fortælle sine kammerater. Hvad der virkelig var sket, ønskede han ikke at fortælle, fordi det forekom ham ikke værd at berette. Han fandt kosakkerne, spurgte efter det regiment, der opererede med Platovs deling, og fandt om aftenen sin herre, Nikolaj Rostov, indkvarteret i Jankovo. Rostov var lige ved at stige til hest for at ride en tur rundt til de omliggende landsbyer med Iljin; han lod Lavrusjka få en anden hest og tog ham med.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: While this was happening in Petersburg, the French had already passed Smolensk and were drawing ever closer to Moscow. Napoleon's historian Thiers, like his other historians, trying to justify his hero, says that Napoleon was drawn to the walls of Moscow against his will. He is as right as other historians who look for the explanation of historic events in the will of one man; he is as right as the Russian historians who maintain that Napoleon was drawn to Moscow by the skill of the Russian commanders. Here, besides the law of hindsight—which treats all the past as preparation for events that subsequently occur—the law of reciprocity comes in, confusing the whole matter. A good chess player who has lost a game is sincerely convinced his loss resulted from a mistake he made and looks for that mistake in the opening, forgetting that at every stage there were similar mistakes and that none of his moves were perfect. He only notices the mistake that catches his attention because his opponent took advantage of it. How much more complex than chess is the game of war, which occurs within limits of time, where it is not one will that moves lifeless objects, but everything results from countless conflicts of various wills!

After Smolensk, Napoleon sought a battle beyond Dorogobutz at Vyazma, and then at Tsarevo-Zaimishche, but it happened that due to a combination of innumerable circumstances, the Russians could not give battle until they reached Borodino, seventy miles from Moscow. From Vyazma, Napoleon ordered a direct advance on Moscow.

Moscow, the Asiatic capital of this great empire, the sacred city of Alexander's people, Moscow with its countless churches shaped like Chinese pagodas—this Moscow gave Napoleon's imagination no rest. On the march from Vyazma to Tsarevo-Zaimishche, he rode his light bay bobtailed horse accompanied by his Guards, his bodyguard, his pages, and his aides-de-camp. Berthier, his chief of staff, dropped behind to question a Russian prisoner captured by the cavalry. Followed by the interpreter Lelorgne d'Ideville, he overtook Napoleon at a gallop and reined in his horse with an amused expression.
* "Moscow, the Asiatic capital of this great empire, the sacred city of Alexander's people, Moscow with its countless churches shaped like Chinese pagodas."
"Well?" asked Napoleon.
"One of Platov's Cossacks says that Platov's corps is joining the main army and that Kutuzov has been appointed commander in chief. He's a very shrewd and talkative fellow."

Napoleon smiled and ordered them to give the Cossack a horse and bring the man to him. He wanted to talk to him personally. Several aides galloped off, and an hour later Lavrushka—the serf Denisov had handed over to Rostov—rode up to Napoleon in an orderly's jacket on a French cavalry saddle, with a cheerful, tipsy face. Napoleon told him to ride alongside and began questioning him.
"Are you a Cossack?"
"Yes, a Cossack, your Honor."

"The Cossack, not knowing in what company he was, for Napoleon's plain appearance had nothing about it that would reveal to an Eastern mind the presence of a monarch, talked with extreme familiarity about the incidents of the war," says Thiers, narrating this episode. In reality, Lavrushka had gotten drunk the day before and left his master without dinner, had been whipped, and was sent to the village to find chickens, where he went looting until the French took him prisoner. Lavrushka was one of those coarse, brazen lackeys who have seen all sorts of things, consider it essential to do everything in a mean and cunning way, are ready to perform any service for their master, and are sharp at guessing their master's baser impulses, especially those driven by vanity and pettiness.
Finding himself in Napoleon's company, whose identity he had easily and surely recognized, Lavrushka was not the least bit intimidated, and simply did his utmost to win his new master's favor.

He knew perfectly well that this was Napoleon, but Napoleon's presence could no more intimidate him than Rostov's, or a sergeant major with a rod, would have done—for he had nothing that either the sergeant major or Napoleon could take from him.

So he rattled on, telling all the gossip he had heard among the orderlies. Much of it was true. But when Napoleon asked whether the Russians thought they would beat Bonaparte or not, Lavrushka squinted and considered.
In this question he detected subtle cunning, as men of his type see cunning in everything, so he frowned and didn't answer right away.
"It's like this," he said thoughtfully. "If there's a battle soon, yours will win. That's right. But if three days pass, then after that, well, that same battle will drag on for a long time."

Lelorgne d'Ideville smilingly translated this to Napoleon as follows: "If a battle takes place within the next three days, the French will win, but if later, God knows what will happen." Napoleon didn't smile, though he was evidently in high good humor, and he ordered the words to be repeated.
Lavrushka noticed this and, to entertain him further, pretending not to know who Napoleon was, added:
"We know you've got Bonaparte and that he's beaten everybody in the world, but we're a different story..."—without knowing why or how this bit of boastful patriotism slipped out at the end.

The interpreter translated these words without the final phrase, and Bonaparte smiled. "The young Cossack made his mighty interlocutor smile," says Thiers. After riding a few paces in silence, Napoleon turned to Berthier and said he wanted to see how the news that he was talking to the Emperor himself—to that very Emperor who had inscribed his immortally victorious name on the Pyramids—would affect this child of the Don.
* "Child of the Don."
The fact was accordingly conveyed to Lavrushka.

Lavrushka, understanding that this was meant to confuse him and that Napoleon expected him to be frightened, promptly pretended to be astonished and awestruck to please his new masters—he opened his eyes wide and put on the expression he usually wore when being led off for a whipping. "As soon as Napoleon's interpreter had spoken," says Thiers, "the Cossack, seized by amazement, did not utter another word but rode on with his eyes fixed on the conqueror whose fame had reached him across the steppes of the East. All his talkativeness was suddenly arrested and replaced by a naive and silent feeling of admiration. Napoleon, after making the Cossack a present, had him set free like a bird restored to its native fields."

Napoleon rode on, dreaming of the Moscow that so captivated his imagination, and "the bird restored to its native fields" galloped back to our outposts, making up along the way all the things that hadn't happened but that he intended to tell his comrades. What had actually happened he didn't care to relate, because it didn't seem worth telling. He found the Cossacks, asked for the regiment operating with Platov's detachment, and by evening found his master Nicholas Rostov, quartered at Yankovo. Rostov was just mounting up for a ride around the neighboring villages with Ilyin; he gave Lavrushka another horse and took him along.
